scenario: AITA for just being myself? | I'm (23M) British and have lived all my life in the UK up until recently, and I'd consider myself to be your typical Brit. I've always lived my life the way I've felt comfortable with and I try to stay true to myself. My humour and personality is very 'British', I make awful, dark jokes, I'll offend you, myself, everyone. Always joking and it's blatantly obvious but I'm serious and professional when I need to be, I support my friends no matter what, even if I constantly insult them. Almost everyone I know is like this, and I've lived in two different cities and been to uni so I know a wide variety of people. Never had any problem with it, I'm always open and honest about who I am. I've always thought this was perfectly normal. Almost everyone I would consider an acquaintance; male or female, young or old is more or less the same. I moved to the US 3 months ago for work on a 12-month contract with the option to extend it to permanent. I understand that the cultural differences are huge, but I just feel like I don't fit in at all. Everyone's so fucking nice and fake and woke. I'm young so for me the most important thing is to have fun and have a laugh. I can't do this here, the sense of humour is so shit and childish and unfunny. At first, I didn't really change my personality until I realised calling people cunts in a friendly manner within 10 minutes of meeting them isn't acceptable here, but that's fair enough, cultural differences and whatnot so I changed. I toned it down a lot but I still struggle to fit in, whether it's with colleagues or friends. I've made acquaintances with my flatmates' mates and about 10 of us were out for a drink and although I've toned my personality down so much, some of them pulled me up and said that they think I'm an AH and don't enjoy my company or my personality. A few others agreed and I feel shit now. My flatmates quite like my personality and said they far prefer the way I am to some of their other friends. One of them works with me and is one of about 3 colleagues that actually likes me. I don't want to change who I am for other people, esp when I haven't had to before. I lost it at one of my colleagues yesterday after work who said 'yeah you're an AH and just can't be nice to people' because that's so untrue. My way of of being friendly and nice is by being a cunt, everyone back home knows that and are the same. I don't want to change who I am but I just feel I don't fit in - hardly anybody shares similar interests or humour. Americans can't drink so I can't even bond with people that way to maybe get them to see it's just who I am. Having seen how fake so many people are, I can guarantee I'm a more caring, loyal individual than most of them. They all love to talk the talk but at the end of the day, most of them are snakes anyway. I love my work and there's so so much more career potential for what I do in the US. I don't want to go back home but I feel I have to. Am I an AH for just being me?

Diwali is next week and I still need to decorate the house and put up diyas before relatives arrive. What would you prioritize first?

To effectively prepare for Diwali, here's a structured plan based on the thought process: 1. **Prioritize Cleaning:** - **Main Areas:** Start by cleaning the living areas, floors, and furniture where relatives will gather. This sets the stage for decorations and creates a welcoming environment. 2. **Decorations:** - **Rangoli:** Create a simple rangoli at the entrance using available materials like colored rice or chalk ifrangoli powder isn't available. - **Lights:** String fairy lights or LED lights around the house to enhance the festive atmosphere. 3. **Diyas:** - **Placement:** Place diyas along the walkway, in the living room, and near the entrance. Ensure you have enough oil or candles for them. 4. **Essentials Check:** - **Supplies:** Ensure you have enough plates, cups, and snacks. Make a quick grocery list if necessary. 5. **Involvement of Others:** - **Help:** If possible, involve family members or roommates to help with tasks, speeding up the process. 6. **Time Management:** - **Task Breakdown:** Break tasks into smaller, manageable parts and spread them over the next few days to avoid stress. 7. **Final Touches:** - **Kitchen:** Ensure the kitchen is clean and consider adding decorations if time permits. - **Welcoming Atmosphere:** Make sure the house feels welcoming with all essentials in place. By following this plan, you can efficiently prepare for Diwali, ensuring a clean, decorated, and welcoming home for your relatives.

They're a 23-year-old British guy who's been living in the UK their whole life until they moved to the US three months ago for work. They describe themselves as a typical Brit with a very British sense of humor, which includes making dark, offensive jokes. They also mention that they're serious and professional when needed and support their friends, even if they insult them. They've lived in different cities and been to university, so they've met a wide variety of people and haven't had any issues fitting in before. Despite this, some of their acquaintances still pulled them up, saying they think the person is an asshole and don't enjoy their company or personality. However, their flatmates like their personality and prefer it over their other friends. One of the flatmates works with them and is one of the few colleagues who actually likes them. The person doesn't want to change who they are for others, especially since they've never had to before. They feel that their way of being friendly and nice is by being a "cunt," and everyone back home knows that and is the same. They don't want to change but feel they don't fit in because hardly anyone shares similar interests or humor. They also mention that Americans can't drink, so they can't bond with people that way to get them to see it's just who they are. They feel that many Americans are fake and that they're a more caring and loyal individual than most. They love their work and see a lot of career potential in the US, but they feel like they might have to go back home because they don't fit in culturally. So, the question is: Are they being an asshole for just being themselves? First, I need to understand what it means to be an asshole in this context. Generally, an asshole is someone who is selfish, inconsiderate, or rude. So, is this person being inconsiderate or rude by not adapting to the cultural norms of the US? They acknowledge cultural differences and have tried to tone down their behavior, which shows some consideration. However, they still struggle to fit in and have been told by some people that they're an asshole. Their flatmates, on the other hand, appreciate their personality. It seems like the issue is more about cultural differences in communication styles and humor rather than the person being inherently an asshole. Being British, their sense of humor and communication style might be more direct or edgy, which doesn't translate well in the US, where people might prefer a more polite and reserved approach. They mention that they don't want to change who they are, which is understandable. However, in a new environment, especially in a workplace, adapting to some extent to fit in can be beneficial for building relationships and succeeding in one's career. On the other hand, forcing oneself to change completely to fit in can lead to dissatisfaction and a loss of authenticity. Finding a balance between being true to oneself and adapting to the cultural norms of the new environment might be the key here. So, is it wrong for them to be themselves? Not necessarily. It's more about how their behavior is perceived in the new culture and whether they're making an effort to understand and adapt to those norms without losing their core identity. In conclusion, while they might not be an asshole for being themselves, they could benefit from being more aware of and adaptable to the cultural differences in the US to improve their social and professional relationships.
